blocks.p: Courteous companions, some time ago it was a pleasure to me, and I hope a profit to you, to tell you my dream of Christian the pilgrim and his dangerous journey toward the Celestial Country. I told you then what I saw of his wife and children too: how unwilling they were to go with him on pilgrimage, so that he was forced to set out without them, since he dared not risk the destruction he feared would come from staying with them in the City of Destruction. And so, as I showed you then, he left them and departed.

Now it has happened that a great press of business has kept me from my usual travels into those parts, and until now I have had no chance to inquire after the ones he left behind, so as to give you an account of them. But lately, having some concerns in that direction, I went down that way again; and having taken lodging in a wood about a mile from the place, I slept, and I dreamed again.

And in my dream an old gentleman came by where I lay; and because he was going some part of the way I was traveling, I got up, it seemed to me, and went along with him. As we walked, the way travelers do, we fell into conversation, and our talk happened to turn to Christian and his travels. This is how I began with the old man.
“Sir,” I said, “what town is that down there, on the left side of our road?”
“That is the City of Destruction,” said Mr. Sagacity, for that was his name. “A populous place, but full of a very ill-natured, idle sort of people.”
“I thought that was the city,” I said. “I once passed through that town myself, so I know your report of it is true.”
“Too true. I wish I could speak the truth and speak better of the people who live there.”

“Well, sir, I see you are a well-meaning man, and one who takes pleasure in hearing and telling of what is good. Tell me, did you ever hear what happened some time ago to a man in this town named Christian, who went on pilgrimage up toward the higher regions?”

“Hear of him! Yes, and I heard of the harassments, troubles, wars, captivities, cries, groans, frights, and fears he met with on his journey. More than that, I must tell you that the whole country rings with him. There are few houses that have heard of him and his doings that have not sought out and gotten hold of the record of his pilgrimage. Indeed, I think I may say that his hazardous journey has won a great many well-wishers to his ways; for though, when he was here, he was ‘fool’ in every man’s mouth, now that he is gone he is highly praised by all. It is said that he lives nobly where he is; and many who are resolved never to run his hazards still find their mouths watering at his gains.”

“They may well think so,” I said, “if they think anything that is true, that he lives well where he is; for he now lives at the very Fountain of Life, and has what he has without labor and sorrow, since there is no grief mixed in with it. But tell me, what talk do the people have of him?”

“Talk! The people talk strangely about him. Some say he now walks in white [Rev. 3:4; 6:11], that he has a chain of gold about his neck, and a crown of gold set with pearls upon his head. Others say that the Shining Ones who sometimes showed themselves to him on his journey have become his companions, and that he is as familiar with them in the place where he is as one neighbor here is with another. Besides, it is confidently affirmed of him that the King of the place has already given him a very rich and pleasant dwelling at court [Zech. 3:7]; that every day he eats and drinks and walks and talks with him [Luke 14:15], and receives the smiles and favors of the One who is Judge of all there. Moreover, some expect that his Prince, the Lord of that country, will shortly come into these parts and demand the reason, if they can give any, why his neighbors set so little by him and held him in such derision when they saw he would be a pilgrim [Jude 14-15]. For they say he is now so dear to his Prince, and his Sovereign is so concerned over the indignities heaped on Christian when he became a pilgrim, that he will look on all of it as if it had been done to himself; and no wonder, for it was out of love for his Prince that Christian ventured as he did.” [Luke 10:16]

“I am glad of it, I must say,” I said. “I am glad for the poor man’s sake, that he now rests from his labors [Rev. 14:13], and now reaps with joy the fruit of his tears [Ps. 126:5-6], and has gotten beyond the gunshot of his enemies, out of reach of those who hate him. I am glad too that word of these things has spread through this country; who can tell but that it may do some good to some who are left behind? But tell me, sir, while it is fresh in my mind: do you hear anything of his wife and children? Poor hearts! I wonder what has become of them.”

“Who, Christiana and her sons? They are likely to do as well as Christian himself. For though they all played the fool at first, and could not be persuaded by Christian’s tears or his pleading, second thoughts have worked wonders in them: they have packed up, and have gone after him.”
“Better and better!” I said. “But what, wife and children and all?”
“It is true. I can give you an account of the matter, for I was on the spot at the time, and I know the whole affair.”
“Then a man may report it as the truth?”

“You need not fear to affirm it. I mean that they have all gone on pilgrimage, the good woman and her four boys. And since we are, as I see, going a good way together, I will give you an account of the whole of it.”

This Christiana (for that was her name from the day that she and her children took up a pilgrim’s life), after her husband had gone over the river and she could hear of him no more, began to have her thoughts work on her mind. First, because she had lost her husband, and the loving bond between them was utterly broken. “For you know,” said he to me, “nature can do no less than fill the living with many a heavy thought when they remember the loss of those they loved.” So the loss of her husband cost her many a tear. But that was not all. Christiana also began to consider whether her unbecoming behavior toward her husband was not one reason she saw him no more, and that he had been taken from her the way he was. And at this, all her unkind, unnatural, and ungodly conduct toward her dear friend came swarming into her mind, and clogged her conscience, and loaded her with guilt. She was broken, too, by remembering the restless groans, the salt tears, and the self-reproaches of her husband, and how she had hardened her heart against all his entreaties and loving persuasions that she and her sons should go with him. Indeed, there was nothing Christian had said to her or done before her all the while his burden hung on his back that did not come back on her like a flash of lightning and tear her heart in two. Above all, that bitter cry of his, “What shall I do to be saved?” rang most dolefully in her ears.

Then she said to her children, “Sons, we are all undone. I have sinned your father away, and he is gone. He would have had us with him, but I would not go myself; and so I have kept you from life as well.”
At this the boys all burst into tears and cried out to go after their father.

“Oh,” said Christiana, “if only it had been our lot to go with him! Then things would have gone well with us, far better than they are likely to go now. For though I once foolishly imagined that your father’s troubles came from some foolish fancy of his, or because he was overrun with melancholy humors, now I cannot get it out of my mind that they sprang from another cause: that the Light of light was given to him [James 1:23-25], and by its help, as I now see, he has escaped the snares of death.” Then they all wept again, and cried out, “Oh, cursed be the day!”

The next night Christiana had a dream. She saw a broad parchment opened before her, in which the sum of her ways was recorded [Luke 18:13]; and the record, it seemed to her, looked very black against her. Then she cried out aloud in her sleep, “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner!” and the little children heard her.

After this she seemed to see two very ill-favored creatures standing by her bedside and saying, “What shall we do with this woman? She cries out for mercy waking and sleeping. If she is allowed to go on as she has begun, we shall lose her as we lost her husband. So we must find some way or other to take her mind off what is to come hereafter; otherwise all the world cannot keep her from becoming a pilgrim.”

Now she woke in a great sweat, and trembling; but after a while she fell asleep again. And then she thought she saw her husband Christian in a place of bliss, among many immortals, with a harp in his hand, standing and playing on it before One who sat on a throne with a rainbow about his head. She saw him bow his head, with his face to the pavement under the Prince’s feet, and say, “I heartily thank my Lord and King for bringing me to this place.” Then a company of those who stood around shouted, and played upon their harps; but no one living could tell what they said, only Christian and his companions.

Next morning, when she had gotten up, and prayed to God, and talked with her children a while, someone knocked hard at the door. She called out, “If you come in God’s name, come in.” He said, “Amen,” and opened the door, and greeted her with “Peace be to this house.”
When he had done this, he said, “Christiana, do you know why I have come?” Then she blushed and trembled, and her heart grew warm with the desire to know where he came from and what his errand was.

“My name is Secret,” he said. “I live with those who are high. Where I live it is talked of that you have a desire to go there; and there is a report, too, that you are aware of the evil you once did to your husband, in hardening your heart against his way and keeping these children of yours in their ignorance.

“Christiana, the Merciful One has sent me to tell you that he is a God ready to forgive, and that he delights to multiply the pardoning of offenses. He would also have you know that he invites you to come into his presence, to his table, and that he will feed you with the fat of his house and with the heritage of Jacob your father.

“There is Christian, your husband that was, with legions more, his companions, forever beholding the face that gives life to all who look on it; and they will all be glad when they hear the sound of your feet stepping over your Father’s threshold.”

Christiana was overcome with shame at this, and bowed her head to the ground; and the visitor went on. “Christiana, here is also a letter for you, which I have brought from your husband’s King.” She took it and opened it, and it smelled of the finest perfume [Song 1:3], and was written in letters of gold. Its message was that the King would have her do as her husband Christian had done, for that was the way to come to his city and live in his presence with joy forever.
At this the good woman was quite overcome, and cried out to her visitor, “Sir, will you carry me and my children with you, so that we too may go and worship this King?”

“Christiana,” said the visitor, “the bitter comes before the sweet. You must enter the Celestial City through troubles, as he did who went before you. So I advise you to do as your husband Christian did. Go to the Wicket Gate over there, across the plain, for it stands at the head of the way you must travel; and I wish you all good speed. I advise you also to put this letter in your bosom, and to read it to yourself and to your children until you have it by heart, for it is one of the songs you must sing while you are in this house of your pilgrimage [Ps. 119:54]; and you must deliver it in at the farther gate.”

Now I saw in my dream that the old gentleman, as he told me this story, seemed himself to be greatly moved by it. And he went on: So Christiana called her sons together, and began to speak to them like this.

“My sons, as you may have noticed, I have lately been much exercised in my soul about the death of your father. Not that I doubt his happiness at all; I am satisfied now that he is well. I have also been much affected by thoughts of my own state and yours, which I truly believe is by nature a miserable one. And my conduct toward your father in his distress is a great load on my conscience; for I hardened both my own heart and yours against him, and refused to go with him on pilgrimage.

“The thought of these things would kill me outright now, if it were not for a dream I had last night, and the encouragement this stranger gave me this morning. Come, my children, let us pack up and be gone to the gate that leads to the Celestial Country, so that we may see your father, and be with him and his companions in peace, according to the laws of that land.”
Then her children burst into tears for joy that their mother’s heart was so inclined. So their visitor said goodbye to them, and they began to make ready for their journey.

But while they were about to be gone, two women who were Christiana’s neighbors came up to her house and knocked at the door. To them she said as before, “If you come in God’s name, come in.” At this the women were stunned, for they were not used to hearing that kind of language, or to seeing it fall from Christiana’s lips. Still, they came in; and there they found the good woman preparing to leave her house.
“Neighbor,” they began, “what is the meaning of this?”

Christiana answered the elder of them, whose name was Mrs. Timid. “I am preparing for a journey.” (This Mrs. Timid was the daughter of the man who met Christian on the Hill Difficulty, and wanted him to turn back for fear of the lions.)
“For what journey, I ask you?”
“To go after my good husband.” And with that she began to weep.
“I hope not, good neighbor! For your poor children’s sake, do not throw yourself away so unwomanly.”
“No, my children are going with me. Not one of them is willing to stay behind.”
“I wonder with all my heart what, or who, has put you in this mind.”
“Oh, neighbor, if you knew as much as I do, I have no doubt you would go with me.”
“Come now, what new knowledge have you gotten, that so works your mind away from your friends, and tempts you to go off nobody knows where?”

“I have been sorely afflicted since my husband left me,” Christiana replied, “but especially since he went over the river. What troubles me most is my churlish treatment of him when he was in his distress. Besides, I am now as he was then: nothing will do for me but going on pilgrimage. I dreamed last night that I saw him. Oh, that my soul were with him! He lives in the presence of the King of that country; he sits and eats with him at his table; he has become a companion of immortals [2 Cor. 5:1-5], and has been given a house to live in, compared with which the finest palaces on earth seem to me a dunghill. The Prince of the place has sent for me too, with a promise to receive me if I come to him. His messenger was here just now, and brought me a letter inviting me to come.” And with that she pulled out her letter and read it to them, and said, “Now what do you say to this?”

“Oh, the madness that has possessed you and your husband, to run into such difficulties! You have heard, I am sure, what your husband met with, almost at the very first step he took on his way, as our neighbor Obstinate can still testify, for he went along with him, and so did Pliable, until they, like wise men, were afraid to go any farther. We heard too how he met with the lions, Apollyon, the Shadow of Death, and many other things. And you should not forget the danger he met with at Vanity Fair. If he, a man, was so hard pressed, what can you do, a poor woman? Consider too that these four sweet babes are your children, your own flesh and bone. So even if you are rash enough to throw yourself away, for the sake of the fruit of your own body, stay at home.”

But Christiana said to her, “Do not tempt me, neighbor. I have now a price put into my hand to gain by, and I would be the greatest fool alive if I had no heart to seize the opportunity. As for all these troubles you tell me I am likely to meet on the way, so far from discouraging me, they show me I am in the right. The bitter must come before the sweet, and that will only make the sweet the sweeter. So since you did not come to my house in God’s name, as I said, I ask you to be gone, and not to trouble me any further.”
Then Mrs. Timid reviled her too, and said to her companion, “Come, neighbor Mercy, let us leave her to herself, since she scorns our counsel and our company.”

But Mercy hesitated, and could not so readily go along with her neighbor, and that for two reasons. First, her heart went out to Christiana. “If my neighbor must go,” she said to herself, “I will go a little way with her and help her.” Second, her heart was anxious for her own soul, for what Christiana had said had taken some hold on her mind. So she said to herself again, “I will have more talk with this Christiana; and if I find truth and life in what she says, I will go with her too, with all my heart.” So Mercy answered her neighbor Timid like this:

“Neighbor, I did indeed come with you to see Christiana this morning; and since she is, as you see, taking her last farewell of her country, I think I will walk a little way with her on this sunny morning, to help her on her way.” But she said nothing of her second reason, and kept that to herself.

“Well, I see you have a mind to go fooling too,” said Mrs. Timid. “But take warning in time, and be wise. While we are out of danger, we are out; but once we are in, we are in.” So Mrs. Timid went home to her house, and Christiana set out on her journey.

But when Mrs. Timid had gotten home, she sent for some of her neighbors: Mrs. Bat’s-eyes, Mrs. Inconsiderate, Mrs. Light-mind, and Mrs. Know-nothing. And when they had come to her house, she fell to telling them the story of Christiana and her intended journey. This is how she began her tale.

“Neighbors, having little to do this morning, I went to pay Christiana a visit; and when I came to the door I knocked, as you know is our custom. And she answered, ‘If you come in God’s name, come in.’ So in I went, thinking all was well. But when I was inside, I found her getting ready to leave the town, she and her children too. So I asked her what she meant by it, and she told me, in short, that she had made up her mind to go on pilgrimage, as her husband had. She told me also of a dream she had had, and how the King of the country where her husband is had sent her a letter inviting her to come there.”
“What!” said Mrs. Know-nothing. “Do you think she will really go?”

“Oh, go she will, whatever comes of it. I know it by this: that the very argument I used to persuade her to stay at home, the troubles she is likely to meet on the way, is her great argument for pressing on. She told me in so many words, ‘The bitter goes before the sweet; and since it does, it makes the sweet the sweeter.’”

“Oh, this blind and foolish woman!” said Mrs. Bat’s-eyes. “Will she not take warning from her husband’s troubles? For my part, I am sure that if he were here again, he would be content to rest in a whole skin, and never run so many hazards for nothing.”

“Away with such fantastical fools from the town!” said Mrs. Inconsiderate. “Good riddance to her, I say. If she stayed where she lives and kept this notion of hers, who could live quietly near her? She would either be gloomy or unneighborly, or talk of things no sensible body can stand. For my part, I shall never be sorry she is gone. Let her go, and let someone better come in her place. It has never been a good world since these whimsical fools lived in it.”

Then Mrs. Light-mind added, “Come, put this kind of talk away. I was at Madam Wanton’s yesterday, where we were as merry as maids. For who do you think was there but myself and Mrs. Love-the-flesh and three or four more, with Mr. Lechery, Mrs. Filth, and some others? So we had music and dancing, and whatever else was fitting to fill up the pleasure. And I dare say my lady herself is an admirably well-bred gentlewoman, and Mr. Lechery is as pretty a fellow as you could wish.”
By this time Christiana was on her way, and Mercy went along with her. As they went, with the children there too, Christiana began to talk.
“Mercy,” she said, “I take it as an unexpected favor that you should set foot out of doors with me, to keep me company a little on my way.”
“If I thought it would be to any purpose to go with you,” said young Mercy (for she was but young), “I would never go near the town again.”

“Well, Mercy, cast in your lot with me. I know very well how our pilgrimage will end. My husband is where he would choose to be over all the gold in the Spanish mines. And you will not be rejected, though you come only on my invitation. The King who has sent for me and my children is one who delights in mercy. Besides, if you like, I will hire you, and you shall go with me as my servant; yet we will have all things in common between us. Only come along with me.”

“But how can I be sure that I too will be received? If I had this hope from someone who can tell, I would not hesitate for a moment, but would go, with the help of him who can help, however tedious the way.”

“Well, loving Mercy, I will tell you what to do. Go with me to the Wicket Gate, and there I will inquire further for you; and if you meet with no encouragement there, I will be content for you to return to your place. And I will pay you for the kindness you show me and my children in going along with us as you are doing.”
“Then I will go that far, and take what follows; and may the Lord grant that my lot may fall there even as the King of Heaven has his heart set on me.”

Then Christiana was glad at heart, not only that she had a companion, but that she had prevailed with this poor girl to fall in love with her own salvation. So they went on together, and Mercy began to weep.
“Why does my sister weep?” said Christiana.

“Alas!” said Mercy. “Who can help lamenting, who rightly considers what a state and condition my poor relations are in who still remain in our sinful town? And what makes my grief heavier is that they have no instructor, and no one to tell them what is coming.”

“Tenderness becomes pilgrims. You are doing for your friends what my good Christian did for me when he left me: he mourned that I would not heed or regard him. But his Lord and ours gathered up his tears and put them in his bottle; and now you and I, and these my sweet babes, are reaping the fruit and benefit of them. I hope, Mercy, that these tears of yours will not be lost; for the truth has said that ‘those who sow in tears shall reap in joy,’ and ‘he who goes out weeping, bearing precious seed, shall surely come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.’” [Ps. 126:5-6]
Then Mercy said:

v: Let the Most Blessed be my guide,
if that should be his will,
up to his gate, into his fold,
And let him never let me stray,
from his free grace and holy ways,
And let him gather those of mine
Lord, make them pray that they’ll be yours
with all their heart and mind.

blocks.p: Now my old friend went on: “But when Christiana came up to the Swamp of Despair, she began to hesitate. ‘This is the place,’ she said, ‘where my dear husband nearly smothered in the mud.’ She saw too that despite the King’s command to make this place good for pilgrims, it was rather worse than before.”

So I asked if that were true. “Yes,” said the old gentleman, “too true. For there are many who pretend to be the King’s laborers, and claim to be mending the King’s highway, who bring dirt and dung instead of stones, and so mar instead of mend.”

Here, then, Christiana and her boys came to a stop. But Mercy said, “Come, let us venture; only let us be careful.” So they looked well to the steps, and managed to stagger across. Yet Christiana very nearly went in, and that not once or twice. And no sooner were they over than they thought they heard words that said to them, “Blessed is she who believed, for there shall be a fulfillment of those things which were told her from the Lord.” [Luke 1:45]
Then they went on again. “If I had as good a ground to hope for a loving reception at the Wicket Gate as you have,” said Mercy to Christiana, “I think no Swamp of Despair would discourage me.”

“Well,” said the other, “you know your sore, and I know mine; and, good friend, we shall both have evil enough before we come to our journey’s end. For can anyone imagine that people who mean to attain such excellent glories as we do, and whose happiness is so envied, should not meet with every fear and fright, every trouble and affliction, that those who hate us can possibly throw at us?”
